d: Loud confused noise from many sources
r: French brouhaha, of disputed origin; possibly Hebrew barúkh habá “welcome”
s: It caused quite a brouhaha when the school suspended one of its top students for refusing to adhere to the dress code.
old_f: A thick stew of brown beans
A light ale brewed in spring
A small house in the hills
ety: Borrowed from French brouhaha, though its earlier origin is disputed. Possibly from Hebrew בָּרוּךְ הַבָּא (barúkh habá, “welcome”, literally “blessed is he who comes”).

d: The necessary means (especially financial means)
r: Where- + withal; used as a noun since about 1800
s: I would like to help your project, but I do not have the wherewithal.
old_f: The exact location (especially of a hidden thing)
The proper reason (especially for an action)
The usual habit (especially of an animal)
ety: From where- + withal. Originally only an adverb, nominal use since ca. 1800.

d: A thin plain-weave cotton or linen fabric; used for shirts or dresses
r: French batiste, a form of Baptiste, of disputed origin
s: He had started to stroke her, shivering, staring ahead, following with a blind man's hand the dip of her spine through the batiste.
old_f: A short wooden club; used by police officers on night patrol
A small flying mammal; used in folk medicine to cure fevers
A rite of washing with water; used to welcome a child into the church
ety: From French batiste, a form of Baptiste, of disputed origin (“according to Littré and Scheler from the alleged original maker, Baptiste of Cambray; according to others, from its use in wiping the heads of children after baptism” – OED).

d: A deceptive maneuver (especially to avoid capture)
r: Latin artificium
s: The notion that consequence can be as easily managed as PR is the ultimate artifice and the ultimate delusion.
old_f: A skilled craft (especially of weaving)
A heavy cannon (especially for sieges)
A formal clause (especially of a treaty)
ety: From Middle French artifice, from Latin artificium.

d: Too obvious to be doubted
r: French indubitable or Latin indubitābilis: in- + dubitable
s: The indubitable effect of the potion convinced many nonbelievers.
old_f: Too heavy to be lifted
Too faint to be heard
Too dirty to be cleaned
ety: Either from French indubitable or Latin indubitābilis. By surface analysis, in- + dubitable.

d: The appearance of truth; the quality of seeming to be true
r: Latin vērīsimilitūdō “likeness to truth”, from vērī “of the true” + similitūdō “likeness”
s: Other adulteries were noted in the interest of verisimilitude.
old_f: The habit of rhyming; the quality of writing in regular verse
The love of green things; the quality of being fresh and full of growth
The fear of heights; the quality of feeling dizzy when looking down
ety: From Middle French vérisimilitude, from Latin vērīsimilitūdō (“likeness to truth”), more correctly written separately as vērī similitūdō; from vērī, genitive singular of vērus (“true, real”), + similitūdō (“likeness, resemblance”).

d: A lover of learning
r: Greek philomathḗs “fond of learning”, from phílos “loving” + máthē “learning”
s: The success of an almanac depended upon the appeal of the "philomath"-the resident astrologer who did the writing and predicting.
old_f: A lover of horses
A lover of music
A lover of stamps
ety: First indubitably attested ante 1643 (perhaps antedated to 1611); from the Ancient Greek φιλομαθής (philomathḗs, “fond of learning”), from φίλος (phílos, “loving”) + μάθη (máthē, “learning”), from μανθάνω (manthánō, “learn”); compare opsimath, philomathematic, and polymath.

d: Deprive of by deceit
r: Origin obscure; possibly nob + -le, or an alteration of nubble
s: Jury trials were reformed to allow majority verdicts, so that criminals could less easily nobble them.
old_f: Make noble
Gnaw at softly
Walk unsteadily
ety: Origin obscure. Possibly from nob + -le, or perhaps an alteration of nubble. Compare also dialectal knobble (“to hit or strike”).

d: A rowdy or mischievous person (usually a young man)
r: An alteration, influenced by hell, of dialectal hallion “scamp, worthless fellow”
s: He chased the young hellions out of his yard.
old_f: A golden statue (usually of the sun god)
A small flowering plant (usually yellow and bright)
A loud greeting (usually shouted across a street)
ety: An alteration, under the influence of hell, of northern English/Scottish dialectal hallion (“scamp, worthless fellow”), of unknown origin.

d: Transfer power to someone
r: French députer, from Latin deputo
s: Some persons, deputed by a meeting.
old_f: Argue a point
Remove a doubt
Clean a wound
ety: From French députer, from Latin deputo.

d: Show, express or direct through movement
r: Latin gesticulor, from gesticulus “a mimic gesture”, diminutive of gestus “gesture”
s: Groups of dancers were wheeling, plunging, and gesticulating while the ogre, more aphasic than before, mumbled at full strength.
old_f: Carry a baby in the womb
Make a joke at another’s expense
Pour wine into a cup
ety: Borrowed from Latin gesticulātus, perfect active participle of gesticulor (“to gesticulate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from gesticulus (“a mimic gesture”), diminutive of gestus (“gesture”), from gerō (“to bear, carry, perform”).

d: A proposal offered for acceptance or rejection
r: Middle English profre “act of offering”
s: "Oh no," she refused demurely at their proffer of coffee.
old_f: A tall stand for reading lectures
A gain made from a sale
A rough draft of a plan
ety: The noun is derived from Middle English profre (“act of offering or presenting a gift; offer of something; challenge; sacrifice; act of petitioning or requesting; petition, request; proposal, suggestion; idea, thought; attempt, effort; appearance; (law) payment to the Exchequer by a sheriff or other officer of estimated revenue due to the monarch”) [and other forms], and then: * partly from Late Latin profrum, proferum (“payment to the Exchequer of estimated revenue due to the monarch (also puruoffrus), offer to convict a criminal”), and from its likely etymon Anglo-Norman profre, proffre, por

d: In a series; one after another
r: Medieval Latin seriatim, from Latin seriēs “row, chain” + -ātim
s: The author then took up each step seriatim of the technique and after-treatment.
old_f: In earnest; with great solemnity
In secret; without being seen
In silence; without a word
ety: From Medieval Latin seriatim, from Latin seriēs (“row, chain”) + -ātim, adverbial suffix.

d: Inspiring fear
r: Anglo-Norman and Middle French redoutable
s: The redoubtable New York Times has been called the “newspaper of record” of the United States.
old_f: Freshly painted
Doubled again
Hard to doubt
ety: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English redoutable (“worthy of honour, venerable; frightening, terrible”), borrowed from Anglo-Norman redoutable and Middle French redoutable, redoubtable, from Old French redotable (modern French redoutable), from redoter (“to fear”) (whence Middle French redoubter, redouter, French redouter) + -able (suffix meaning ‘deserving of, worthy of’). Redoter is derived from re- (intensifying prefix) + doter (“to doubt; to fear”) (from Latin dubitō (“to doubt, be uncertain, waver in opinion”), probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dwi- (“apart, asunde

d: Unhappy in love; suffering from unrequited love
r: Love + lorn
s: Ye artists lovelorn! madmen that ye are.
old_f: Happy in love; recently engaged to be married
Lost in thought; dreaming of far-off places
Worn by age; faded from long use
ety: From love + lorn.

d: Characterized by propriety and dignity and good taste in manners and conduct
r: Latin decōrus “becoming, fitting, proper”, from decor “elegance, grace”
s: Rome appears to keep awake and stirring, though in a quiet and decorous way.
old_f: Characterized by elaborate ornament and gilding in furnishings and dress
Characterized by a tendency to give in to temptation and pleasure
Characterized by gradual decay and the loss of strength and vigor
ety: From the following: * Latin decōrus (“becoming, fitting, proper, suitable”) + English -ous (suffix adjectives denoting presence of a quality in any degree, typically an abundance). Decōrus is derived from decor (“elegrance, grace; charm beauty”) + -us (suffix forming adjectives); and decor is from decēre, the present active infinitive of decet (“to adorn; to be decent; to be proper or suitable”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *deḱ- (“to perceive; to take”). * Possibly also influenced by Late Latin decorōsus (“beautiful; elegant”), from decoris + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of’ forming ad

d: Stubbornly unyielding
r: Old French pertinace, from Latin pertinax, from per- “very” + tenax “tenacious”
s: The most vocal and pertinacious of all the critics.
old_f: Highly relevant
Deeply troubled
Greatly angered
ety: From pertinace + -ious, from Old French pertinace, from Latin pertinax, from per- (“very”) + tenax (“tenacious”).

d: A feeling of anger caused by being offended
r: Middle French ombrage, from Latin umbrāticus “in the shade”, from umbra “shadow, shade”
s: She looked very neurotic, moving in a jerky way, her body giving little twitches of habitual umbrage.
old_f: A covering of oiled cloth carried to keep off rain
A deep brown pigment made from earth
A feeling of pride caused by being praised
ety: From Middle French ombrage (“umbrage”), from Old French ombrage, from Latin umbrāticus (“in the shade”), from umbra (“shadow, shade”).

d: Full and loud and deep
r: Latin sonōrus, from sonor “sound”
s: He was selected to give the opening speech thanks to his imposing, sonorous voice.
old_f: Sleepy and slow to wake
Bitter and sour to taste
Sweet and soft as silk
ety: Borrowed from Latin sonōrus, from sonor (“sound”), early 17th century.

d: A solid section between two crenels in a crenelated battlement
r: French merlon, from Italian merlone, from merlo; possibly from Latin merula “blackbird”
s: The castle spread out before him, its high solid sandstone walls, with their crenel and merlon battlements ending in round towers, was a magnificent sight.
old_f: A small dark songbird that nests between two rocks in a stone wall
A wild sea creature that is half woman and half fish in folk tales
A narrow slit between two stones through which archers shoot
ety: Borrowed from French merlon, from Italian merlone (“merlon”), from merlo (“merlon”) + -one (suffix forming augmentatives). Merlo is derived from Late Latin merulus, merlus, possibly from Latin merula (“blackbird”) (as merlons resemble a row of birds perched on a wall), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ems- (“black; blackbird”). The English word is cognate with Italian mergolo (“battlement; pinnacle”), Portuguese merlão, Spanish merlón (“merlon”).

d: One retired from society for religious reasons
r: Greek anakhōrētḗs, from anakhōréō “to withdraw, retire”, via Latin anchōrēta
s: Oh, hang him? He's a very Anchorite—a young Hermit!
old_f: One who sails ships for a living
One who keeps the family records
One who tells stories in public
ety: From Ancient Greek ἀναχωρητής (anakhōrētḗs, “anchorite”), from ἀναχωρέω (anakhōréō, “to withdraw, retire”), via Latin anchōrēta, a variant of anachōrēta (“anchorite”), see -ite.

d: Surpassing the ordinary or normal
r: Preter- + natural, after Latin praeter nātūram “beyond nature”
s: Macbeth is like a record of a preternatural and tragical event.
old_f: Existing before birth
Feigned for show
Fond of the outdoors
ety: From preter- + natural, after Latin prēternātūrālis/praeternātūrālis, from praeter nātūram, from praeter (“beyond”) + nātūra (“nature”); compare supernatural.

d: A document entitling a commissioned officer to hold a higher rank temporarily (but without higher pay)
r: Anglo-Norman diminutive of bref “letter”, from Latin brevis “short”
s: Fine chance for promotion, it seems—aye, a stove boat will make me an immortal by brevet.
old_f: A short sermon (often written in Latin) that a priest reads at a funeral or memorial
A small loaf (often made of rye) that is given to soldiers at the start of a march
A light jacket (often lined with fur) that cavalry officers wear over one shoulder
ety: Inherited from the Middle English brevet (“official letter”), from the Anglo-Norman diminutive of bref (“letter”), from the Latin brevis (“short”), whence brief.

d: An expression of strong disapproval; pronouncing as wrong or morally culpable
r: Dis- + approbation
s: Her feelings must be hurt by such disapprobation.
old_f: A careful testing of a new recruit; examining someone’s fitness for duty
A sudden loss of wealth or rank; falling from a position of high honor
A gentle teasing of a close friend; making light of a shared mistake
ety: From dis- + approbation.

d: The chief steward or butler of a great household
r: Old French seneschal, from Frankish *siniskalk, from *siniz “senior” + *skalkaz “servant”
s: Beside stood seneschals, the appointed witnesses of the ensuing games.
old_f: The chief judge or magistrate of a small town
The eldest son or heir of a noble family
The head monk or abbot of a large monastery
ety: From Middle English seneschal (recorded in English since 1393), from Old French seneschal, from Medieval Latin siniscalcus, from Frankish *siniskalk, from Proto-Germanic *siniskalkaz, from Proto-Germanic *siniz (“senior”) + *skalkaz (“servant”); latter term as in marshal. As an officer of the French crown, via French sénéchal.

d: An opening (in a wall or ship or armored vehicle) for firing through
r: French embrasure, from embraser, from Old French “cut at a slant”
s: The walls are slitted with embrasures through which bowmen could fire.
old_f: A warm embrace (between friends or family) on meeting or parting
A coal fire (in a forge or kitchen) kept burning through the night
A raised platform (in a hall or chapel) for speakers to stand on
ety: From French embrasure, from embras(er) + -ure, from Old French embrasure (“cut at a slant, make a groove or furrow”), from em- + braser (“cut at a slant”).

d: Disposed to believe on little evidence
r: Latin crēdulus “that easily believes”, from crēdō “to believe”
s: The doctor was a small, black, plump man with fuzzy hair and round, credulous eyes.
old_f: Deserving of praise and honor
Having a strong sense of duty
Disposed to cruelty and harshness
ety: Originated in 1576, borrowed from Latin crēdulus (“that easily believes a thing, credulous”), from crēdō (“to believe”).

d: Headdress of cloth; worn over the head and around the neck and ears by medieval women
r: Old English wimpel “veil; a covering for the neck”
s: To envisage with accuracy the appearance of the wimple or the other items that went to make up the habit.
old_f: Basket of willow; carried on the back by peasant women at harvest to gather grapes in the vineyards
Ripple on water; made by fish rising at dusk to feed on insects at the surface
Dimple in the cheek; seen when children laugh and often thought a sign of good luck
ety: From Middle English wympel, wimpel, from Old English wimpel (“veil, an article of women's dress; a covering for the neck, a cloak, a hood”), from Proto-Germanic *wimpilaz (“wimple, scarf, veil”). Cognate with Scots wympill (“wimple”), Dutch wimpel (“streamer, pennant”), German Wimpel (“pennant”), Swedish vimpel (“pennant, banner”), Icelandic vimpill (“hood, cowl”).

d: Only partly in existence; imperfectly formed
r: Latin incipiēns, present participle of incipiō “begin”
s: After 500 years, incipient towns appeared.
old_f: Lacking any flavor; bland and dull
Capable of cutting; sharp and keen
Not yet received; still owed
ety: Borrowed from Latin incipiēns, present participle of incipiō (“begin”).

d: Prove to be false
r: Middle French confuter, from Latin confūtō
s: We can look up something in a book and learn it perfectly well with no other motive than to confute reinforcement theory.
old_f: Throw into disorder
Combine into one
Play on a flute
ety: From Middle French confuter, from Latin confūtō.

d: (usually followed by ‘for’) extremely desirous
r: Old English ofþyrst, past participle of ofþyrstan “to smart from thirst”
s: O sleepless heart and sombre soul unsleeping, That were athirst for sleep and no more life.
old_f: (usually of sailors) blown off course
(usually of fruit) overripe and soft
(usually of a road) crossing at angles
ety: Inherited from Middle English athirst, from Old English ofþyrst, past participle of ofþyrstan (“to smart from thirst”), equivalent to a- (“of”, Etymology 8) + thirst (verb).

d: Curved down like an eagle’s beak
r: Latin aquilīnus, from aquila “eagle”
s: Frank's aquiline nose jutted out from underneath his glasses.
old_f: Pale blue like clear water
Flat and broad like a duck’s bill
Long and thin like a heron’s neck
ety: From Latin aquilīnus, from aquila (“eagle”).

d: Someone who uses a divining rod to find underground water
r: Dowse + -er
s: If you look closely you may see it suggested that she is a “sensitive” of some kind, a dowser in the world of global marketing.
old_f: Someone who puts out fires by throwing buckets of water
Someone who sleeps lightly in a chair after dinner
Someone who arranges marriages for a fee or a dowry
ety: From dowse + -er.

d: A predisposition in favor of something
r: Medieval Latin praedīlēctiō
s: Youth’s predilection for revolt.
old_f: A formal statement made before a vote
A speech of farewell to a departing friend
A blessing spoken over a meal
ety: Borrowed from Medieval Latin praedīlēctiō.

d: Hold back to a later time
r: Old French proroguer, from Latin prōrogō “prolong, defer”
s: The King settled to prorogue Parliament until the Christmas holidays, and to do nothing else for the present.
old_f: Argue in favor of
Rule by royal decree
Speak before a play
ety: From Old French proroger, proroguer, from Latin prōrogō (“prolong, defer”).

d: Fondle or pet affectionately
r: Uncertain; perhaps a blend of caress + noodle “to fool around”
s: He’s got a big smile on his face—who’s he been canoodling recently?
old_f: Paddle a small boat
Doze off briefly
Boil soft pasta
ety: The origin of the verb is uncertain; the following possibilities have been suggested: * From a blend of ca(ress) + noodle (“to engage in frivolous behavior; to fool around or waste time; to mess around, to play”). * From German knuddeln (“to cuddle; (originally) to embrace tightly”); or related to Low German knuddle (“a clump, a knot”), a diminutive of knude, related to Old High German knodo, knoto (“a knot”) (modern German Knoten (“knot”)); ultimate etymology unknown. Compare also Norwegian Bokmål knulle (“to fuck”), Swedish knulla (“to fuck”), both from Proto-Germanic *knuzlijaną (“to beat;

d: Something of little value or significance
r: French friperie, from Old French fripier “to rub up and down, wear into rags”
s: We detest the affectation and effeminate frippery which is but too frequent in the modern novel.
old_f: A sweet fried cake of dough
A sudden fright or scare
A heavy fall of sleet
ety: From French friperie, from Old French fripier (“to rub up and down, to wear into rags”). Compare fripper.

d: A thief who steals from the pockets or purses of others in public places
r: Middle English cutte-purs: cut + purse, since purses hung from a strap at the girdle
s: A cutpurse of the empire and the rule.
old_f: A tailor who makes purses and pouches from the leather offcuts of a saddler’s shop
A barber who cuts hair and pulls teeth in the market squares of country towns
A banker who changes foreign coins for travelers at the gates of walled cities
ety: From Middle English cutte-purs; equivalent to cut + purse: originally, purses were worn by a strap at the girdle, which the thief would cut.

d: An obsolete kind of container used for distillation; two retorts connected by a tube
r: French alambic, from Arabic al-ʔinbīq, from Greek ámbix “cup, cap of a still”
s: Thus is Art, a nature passed through the alembic of man.
old_f: An ancient kind of lamp used for reading; two wicks joined by a brass chain
A medieval kind of crossbow used for hunting; two strings joined by a bar
A sacred kind of bowl used for blessing; two handles joined by a rim
ety: From French alambic, from Medieval Latin alembīcus, from Arabic الإِنْبِيق (al-ʔinbīq), from Ancient Greek ἄμβιξ (ámbix, “cup, cap of a still”). Doublet of ambix and lambic.

d: An embankment built around a space for defensive purposes
r: Middle Dutch bolwerk: bole “tree trunk” + work; a doublet of boulevard
s: The party stalwarts constitute the bulwark that ensures the president's term of office.
old_f: A wide avenue lined with trees for strolling and parades
A heavy beam used to bar the gates of a town
A large pen used to hold bulls before market
ety: From Middle English bulwerk, from Middle Dutch bolwerk, bolwerc and Middle Low German bolwerk, equivalent to bole (“tree trunk”) + work. Cognate with German Bollwerk, Danish bolværk, Swedish bålverk, Dutch bolwerk. Doublet of boulevard (from French boulevard, from Dutch); cognate with Portuguese and Spanish baluarte and Italian baluardo.
